# The shape of the typist

::: {.callout-note}
# Source

A reader's guide to part of [CS 329Z Lecture 2](https://web.stanford.edu/class/cs329z/slides/lecture02.pdf){.external target="_blank"} (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan and John Yang; [Engineering AI Agents](https://cs329z.stanford.edu/){.external target="_blank"}, Stanford, autumn 2026). The outline and the pointers come from that lecture; the wording on this page is ours. The course is also listed under [Resources](resources.qmd#cs329z).
:::


Once you know that a language model is a next-token distribution, the next question is what computes it. The architecture is the typist's memory: how much of the past they can see, how much that look-back costs, and what they have to throw away to go faster.

This page follows the lecture's short history, then the Transformer, then linear attention and the hybrid designs that try to keep both.

::: {.callout-tip}
# Everyday example

Think of reading a long letter. Full attention is like being able to glance back at every earlier sentence whenever you need it: accurate, and slower as the letter grows. A recurrent model is like keeping only a short mental note of what has been said; cheap, and easy to forget a name from page one. Linear attention is a compressed notebook of constant size: you can keep writing for a long time without the notebook getting thicker, but the notes are a summary, not the original pages. A lot of current systems keep a few "glance back at everything" pages and use the notebook for the rest.
:::

# A brief history

The lecture's sketch is short on purpose:

- *N-gram* models (the standard toolkit well into the 2000s, and in use long before) guess the next word from a fixed window of previous words. They are simple, and they hit a wall: a slightly longer phrase, or a slightly new wording, and the table has never seen it.
- The first widely cited *neural language model* is Bengio, Ducharme, Vincent and Jauvin, [A Neural Probabilistic Language Model](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/volume3/bengio03a/bengio03a.pdf){.external target="_blank"} (JMLR, 2003). Words become vectors; a network shares parameters across contexts instead of storing a giant sparse table.
- *Recurrent* neural language models, associated in the lecture with work around 2010 (Mikolov and colleagues), fold the past into a hidden state that is updated token by token.
- *Long short-term memory* was introduced by Hochreiter and Schmidhuber in 1997. The lecture's phrase is that it was popularised for language models in 2014 — a fair mid-2010s date for the wave of LSTM language models and sequence-to-sequence work, not the date the cell was invented.

Then the field changed shape.

# Transformers

[Attention Is All You Need](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762){.external target="_blank"} (Vaswani, Shazeer, Parmar, Uszkoreit, Jones, Gomez, Kaiser and Polosukhin, 2017) replaced recurrence with self-attention. Each token can look at the others in the sequence (with a causal mask, if you are generating left to right), in parallel during training. The original paper is an encoder–decoder model for translation. Almost every chatbot you meet today is a *decoder-only* Transformer: embeddings, positional information, blocks of masked self-attention and a feed-forward network, then a softmax over the vocabulary.

We already have a slower walk through that paper on [Attention Is All You Need](../generative/attention-is-all-you-need.qmd), and a longer arc on the [evolution of attention](../generative/evolution-of-attention.qmd). The lecture figure below is the 2017 diagram with a teaching annotation that marks the encoder and the decoder.

# Linear attention

Softmax attention is $O(n^2)$ in the context length, and the KV cache grows with $n$. That is a tax every agent pays when the transcript, the tools, and the files pile up.

*Linear attention* drops the softmax. In the formulation of [Katharopoulos, Vyas, Pappas and Fleuret, Transformers are RNNs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.16236){.external target="_blank"} (2020), a kernel feature map lets you rewrite attention so that you can maintain a constant-size state and run in $O(n)$ time. The lecture's comparison is the one to keep:

::: {.fig-on-white}
![Full softmax attention versus linear attention: quadratic look-back and a growing KV cache, against a linear scan over a compressed state — CS 329Z Lecture 2 (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan, John Yang), [slide p. 87](https://web.stanford.edu/class/cs329z/slides/lecture02.pdf#page=87){.external target="_blank"}. Lecture original.](/images/agents-l2/arch-softmax-vs-linear-attention.png){#fig-l2-softmax-vs-linear fig-alt="A two-column comparison of full softmax attention and linear attention, covering complexity, how tokens refer to the past, long-context behaviour, and memory." .lightbox fig-align="center" width="100%"}
:::


```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
  X["Tokens in a long context"] --> S["Softmax attention"]
  X --> L["Linear attention"]
  S --> S1["Each new token can look at every earlier token"]
  S --> S2["Time and KV memory grow with n squared and n"]
  L --> L1["Each new token updates a compressed state"]
  L --> L2["Time is linear; memory can stay constant"]
  S1 --> H["Many systems use both"]
  L1 --> H
```

The gain is speed and memory. The cost, which the lecture shows with [RULER](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.06654){.external target="_blank"} (Hsieh et al., 2024), is long-context quality: a compressed state is a worse look-back than attending to the original tokens. A useful side note from the lecture: neither the Transformer nor linear attention *forces* a hard context limit by itself. What usually caps you is how the model was trained to use its positional embeddings. In practice you are limited to the context length the model learned.

# Mixing the two

So people mix them. Some layers, or some heads, keep global softmax attention; the rest use a linear or similarly cheap recurrence. The lecture illustrates this with figures credited to Songlin Yang, *DeltaNet Explained (Part III)* — the same line of work that sits behind [flash-linear-attention](https://github.com/fla-org/flash-linear-attention){.external target="_blank"} — and with a recent hybrid, [Kimi K3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24653){.external target="_blank"} (Moonshot, 2026).

::: {.fig-on-white}

Original: [Kimi K3: Open Frontier Intelligence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24653){.external target='_blank'}.](/images/agents-l2/arch-kimi-k3-mixed-attention.png){#fig-l2-kimi-k3 fig-alt="A diagram of the Kimi K3 hybrid architecture, mixing attention mechanisms." .lightbox fig-align="center" width="100%"}

# Why this matters for agents

The lecture closes the architecture section with a builder's list, not a theorist's:

- Agents meet extremely long contexts.
- Inference efficiency is a design choice, not a later optimisation.
- Knowing the architecture helps you pick a model whose memory and attention pattern fit the job.
- The harness around the model should play to its strengths and cover its weaknesses. That is the job of an agent engineer, and it is the subject of [LLMs for agents](llms-for-agents.qmd).

# In one table

| Architecture | What it keeps of the past | Cost of a longer context |
|--------------|---------------------------|--------------------------|
| N-gram | A fixed window of previous tokens | Tables blow up; unseen phrases get no help |
| RNN / LSTM | A hidden state, updated token by token | Cheap per step; information has to survive the state |
| Softmax Transformer | Every earlier token, via the KV cache | Time $O(n^2)$, memory $O(n)$ |
| Linear attention | A compressed, often constant-size state | Time $O(n)$; weaker long-context recall |
| Hybrid (e.g. mixed global + linear) | A few full look-backs, plus a cheap state | A compromise, now common in practice |

# FAQ

**Why did Transformers replace LSTMs for language models?**
Training can be parallel across the sequence, the path from a token far back is short, and in the mid-2010s that combination scaled better. The 2017 paper's Table 1 is still a clean statement of the tradeoff.

**If linear attention is faster, why keep softmax attention at all?**
Because the cheap state is a summary. Benchmarks such as RULER show that long-context work still benefits from being able to look at the original tokens. Hybrids are an attempt to have both.

**Is the context window a law of the architecture?**
Not in the strict sense the lecture is careful about. Attention does not forbid a longer sequence. What usually binds you is the positional scheme the model was trained with, plus the memory bill of the KV cache.

**Where should I go for the attention equations?**
The lecture walks through queries, keys, values, the causal mask, and multi-head attention. We unpack the same maths in [Attention Is All You Need](../generative/attention-is-all-you-need.qmd). This page stays with the design choices that leak into agents.
